**Answer: $C = \dfrac{2\pi}{|\Omega|}$**, where $|\Omega|$ is the Lebesgue measure (area) of $\Omega$.

**Derivation.** Let $f = \log w$, so $\Delta f = C$ on $\Omega$. The kernel splits as
$$\log\frac{w(x)w(y)}{|x-y|} = f(x) + f(y) - \log|x-y|.$$
Suppose $0$ is an eigenvalue, so there is $u \in L^2(\Omega)$, $u \neq 0$, with $\mathcal{L}_w u = 0$. Define
$$A = \int_\Omega u\,dy, \qquad B = \int_\Omega f u\,dy, \qquad V(x) = \int_\Omega \log|x-y|\,u(y)\,dy.$$
Then $\mathcal{L}_w u = f A + B - V$, so $\mathcal{L}_w u = 0$ gives $V = Af + B$ on $\Omega$.

Take the Laplacian of both sides. Since $\Delta \log|x| = 2\pi\delta$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the distributional Laplacian of $V$ (with $u$ extended by zero outside $\Omega$) is $\Delta V = 2\pi u$ on $\Omega$. The right side gives $\Delta(Af + B) = AC$. Hence
$$u = \frac{AC}{2\pi} \quad \text{a.e. on } \Omega,$$
so $u$ is a constant $c$.

Now impose consistency with the definition of $A$: $A = \int_\Omega u = c|\Omega|$, and $c = \dfrac{AC}{2\pi} = \dfrac{c|\Omega| C}{2\pi}$.

If $c = 0$, then $u = 0$, which is excluded. So $c \neq 0$, and dividing by $c$ gives $|\Omega|\,C = 2\pi$.

This is a necessary condition. The eigenfunction is $u \equiv$ const, and one still needs $V - Af$ to be constant on $\Omega$, which constrains $w$ but does not change the value of $C$.

ANSWER: $C = \dfrac{2\pi}{|\Omega|}$
